O passado: ideia geral e a «tesourinha»: The past: the general idea and the "scissors"
Antes de começar: uma verdade sobre o ru: Before we start, an honest word about Russian. You already know how to conjugate verbs in the present. You know the scissors. You know the pronouns. You know the adverbs (вчера, сегодня, завтра). Now comes the final step: talking about what happened and what is going to happen. But first, an important point that is rarely said honestly: the Russian past you learn here is the past of actions in progress. It does not tell you that an action was finished and closed. It tells you that something was going on, was repeated, or lasted. It is the English "I was reading", "I used to work", "I lived" (without saying how it ended). Likewise, the Russian future you learn here is the future of an action that will go on or repeat, without a marked end: "I will be reading", "I will work", "I will live". This is fundamental for understanding what you are learning. You are not learning "the" past of Russian; you are learning one past, the one for actions in progress, repeated actions and actions without a marked end. Later, when you are ready, you will find another past and another future (the "completed" pair, which says "I read it through", "I will finish reading it"). That is for another time. For now, stay with this one. The good news: this past and this future are the most used in everyday speech. They are the basis of storytelling. With them you can already tell your life. Let's go. PART 1: THE PAST. The scissors rule for the past. You already know the scissors of the present: cut -ТЬ from the infinitive. You have the stem. Paste on the personal ending of the present. The past uses the same scissors with one difference: the past ending does not depend on the person. It depends on the gender. English is the opposite. In English the past form is the same for everyone ("I read, you read, she read"); Russian ignores the person but marks the gender. There are four past endings. That is all. Four endings. Nothing more.
A regra da tesourinha do passado: The scissors rule for the past
A grande diferença do russo. Aqui está a: The big difference in Russian. Here is the most important thing you need to understand: in the present, the verb agrees with the PERSON. In the past, the verb agrees with the GENDER of the subject. Compare. PRESENT (agrees with the person): Я чита́ю. (I read.) Ты чита́ешь. (You read.) Он чита́ет. (He reads.) Она́ чита́ет. (She reads.) Мы чита́ем. (We read.) PAST (agrees with the gender): Я чита́л. (I was reading, if I am a man.) Я чита́ла. (I was reading, if I am a woman.) Ты чита́л. (You were reading, if you are a man.) Ты чита́ла. (You were reading, if you are a woman.) Он чита́л. (He was reading: masculine.) Она́ чита́ла. (She was reading: feminine.) Оно́ чита́ло. (It was reading: neuter.) Мы чита́ли. (We were reading: any gender.) Вы чита́ли. (You were reading: any gender.) Они́ чита́ли. (They were reading: any gender.) Notice: in the singular, the ending changes with the gender. In the plural it is always -ЛИ, whatever the gender. This means that if you are a man and you say "I was reading", it is я чита́л. If you are a woman and you say "I was reading", it is я чита́ла. A man never says «я чита́ла». A woman never says «я чита́л». It is automatic: you do not think "I am a man, I will use -л". You simply use the form that matches you. (In English you only see a trace of this in pronouns: he/she. In Russian a woman talking about herself has to say it in the verb.)
A pergunta mais comum: \"se um homem per: The most common question: "if a man asks a woman, is it -Л or -ЛА?" Every learner has this doubt. Let's answer it clearly. There is one rule and it always holds: the past ending agrees with the GENDER OF THE SUBJECT, that is, of the person who does the action. It does not matter who asks, or who speaks. What matters is who is spoken about. Let me break it down with examples. Situation 1: a man asks a woman: — Ты чита́ла вчера́? (Were you reading yesterday?) The man is asking a woman. The woman is the subject of the sentence (she is the one who was reading), so the ending is -ЛА. The man used -ЛА because he is referring to her, not to himself. The woman answers: — Да, я чита́ла. (Yes, I was.) She answers with -ЛА because she is a woman. She agrees with herself. Situation 2: a woman asks a man: — Ты чита́л вчера́? (Were you reading yesterday?) The woman is asking a man. The man is the subject, so the ending is -Л. The woman used -Л because she is referring to him. The man answers: — Да, я чита́л. (Yes, I was.) He answers with -Л because he is a man. Situation 3: a man asks another man: — Ты чита́л вчера́? — Да, я чита́л. Both use -Л because both are men. Situation 4: a woman asks another woman: — Ты чита́ла вчера́? — Да, я чита́ла. Both use -ЛА because both are women. The rule in one sentence: the past ending does not belong to the speaker. It belongs to the subject of the sentence. If the subject is male, it is -Л. If the subject is female, it is -ЛА. No matter who asks, who answers, or the gender of the other person. More examples to fix it in your mind follow. Notice the last pair: a man talking about a woman uses -ЛА (the subject is she, a woman). A woman talking about a man uses -Л (the subject is he, a man). The gender of the speaker does not matter. What matters is the gender of the subject. Another example, with the verb быть: A man says: Я был до́ма. (I was at home.) A woman says: Я была́ до́ма. (I was at home.) A man asks a woman: Ты была́ до́ма? (Were you at home?) A woman asks a man: Ты был до́ма? (Were you at home?) Always the same logic: the ending follows the subject, not the speaker.

No presente não há «ser/estar» («Я студе: In the present there is no "to be" in Russian («Я студент»). In the past it appears and changes with the gender and number of the SUBJECT: «был» (masculine), «была» (feminine), «было» (neuter), «были» (plural). The speaker counts too: a man says «Я был дома», a woman says «Я была дома». To say "I had", replace «есть» with «был/была/было/были» and agree with the thing you had: «У меня был брат», «У меня была сестра». The negative uses «не было» and the genitive: «У меня не было сестры». At this level we use the everyday past; the difference between the two aspects of the verb will come in a lesson of its own.

Exemplos com verbos regulares. Vamos apl: Examples with regular verbs. Let's apply the scissors to eight regular verbs. Notice the translations: all of them describe an action in progress, repeated or lasting. ЧИТАТЬ (to read): stem ЧИТА-. ГОВОРИТЬ (to speak): stem ГОВОР-. РАБОТАТЬ (to work): stem РАБОТА-. ЖИТЬ (to live): stem ЖИ-. Attention: жить is irregular in the stress; in the feminine the stress goes to the end: жила́, not «жи́ла». ЗНАТЬ (to know): stem ЗНА-. ЛЮБИТЬ (to love): stem ЛЮБ-. СМОТРЕТЬ (to watch, look): stem СМОТРЕ-. ПИСАТЬ (to write): stem ПИСА-. English past forms ("read", "spoke", "worked") never change, but all these Russian forms do.
The most important irregular verbs. A few verbs do not follow the rule. Here are the main ones. БЫТЬ (to be): the most important. This is the verb you use when you want to say "I was at home" (Я был до́ма / Я была́ до́ма). ИДТИ (to go on foot): the most famous of the irregulars. Attention: the verb идти becomes шёл in the past. The stem is completely different, a linguistic fossil. Memorise it. МОЧЬ (can, to be able): мог, могла́, могло́, могли́. ЕСТЬ (to eat): ел, е́ла, е́ло, е́ли. ПИТЬ (to drink): пил, пила́, пи́ло, пи́ли. (English irregular verbs, like "go / went" and "eat / ate", are the same kind of fossil.)
Erros comuns e frases no passado: Common mistakes and sentences in the past
Os erros que o brasileiro VAI cometer no: The mistakes English speakers WILL make in the past. Mistake 1: using the present, or looking for a person ending. ❌ Wrong: Я чита́ю вчера́. ✅ Right: Я чита́л вчера́. (a man) / Я чита́ла вчера́. (a woman). English speakers instinctively think "I read" and look for an "I" form of the past. It does not exist. The Russian past has no person. It has gender. Mistake 2: using -л for a woman. ❌ Wrong: Она́ чита́л вчера́. ✅ Right: Она́ чита́ла вчера́. If the subject is a woman, the ending is -ла, always. Mistake 3: using -л for a plural. ❌ Wrong: Они́ чита́л вчера́. ✅ Right: Они́ чита́ли вчера́. If the subject is plural, the ending is -ли, always, whatever the gender. Mistake 4: thinking that «я был» means "I am". ❌ Wrong: Я был брази́лец, meaning "I am Brazilian". ✅ Right: Я брази́лец (present, with no verb). Я был брази́лец (past: I was Brazilian). «Я был» means "I was". It never means "I am". For "I am", the verb does not appear: «я брази́лец». Mistake 5: not changing the form of быть for a woman. If you are a woman, never say «я был». Say «я была́». Always. Mistake 6: forgetting that идти becomes шёл. ❌ Wrong: Я идти́л вчера́. (It does not exist.) ✅ Right: Я шёл вчера́. (I was going yesterday.) The verb идти is irregular. The stem changes completely in the past. Mistake 7: using your own gender when you ask someone else. ❌ Wrong: A man asks a woman «Ты чита́л?» (using -л because he is a man). ✅ Right: A man asks a woman «Ты чита́ла?» (using -ла because she is a woman). This is the subtlest mistake. English speakers tend to use their own gender ending when asking a question, because in English the speaker's sex never affects the verb. But the ending follows the subject, not the person asking. If a man asks a woman, he uses -ла (because she is a woman). If a woman asks a man, she uses -л (because he is a man). Sentences in the past. Now real sentences, with adverbs of time. Notice the translations: all of them describe actions in progress or repeated. PART 2: THE FUTURE.

Para o passado de quase todo verbo, tire: For the past of almost every verb, take the -ть off the infinitive and add -л (masculine), -ла (feminine), -ло (neuter) or -ли (plural): работать → работал, работала, работало, работали. The past does not change with the person (я, ты, он...), only with the gender and number of the subject. A man says «я читал», a woman says «я читала». Verbs in -ся keep the -ся: просыпался, просыпалась, просыпались. There are very common irregulars, such as «идти» → шёл, шла, шли.
O passado concorda com o gênero de quem: The past agrees with the gender of the person who does the action.
